item.title: Economists concerned after labour market sheds jobs for third month in a row
item.description: Canada’s unemployment rate went up to a six-month high in October and the economy lost a few thousand jobs as the private sector and full-time employment saw declines, data showed on Friday.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: OTTAWA — Some economists are getting worried that a string of job losses in recent months is revealing cracks in the labour market. Statistics Canada said Friday that the unemployment rate rose two tenths of a point to 6.7 per cent in October. The labour market shed 4,700 jobs last month, the agency said, and more people were also looking for work. October’s modest decline followed a cumulative loss of 110,000 jobs across September and August. A Reuters poll of economists had expected the economy would bounce back with a gain of 13,600 jobs in October. “For anyone hoping that October would bring a recovery in the Canadian job market after back-to-back negative surprises, today’s release is a disappointment,” said Sneha Puri, economist with jobs search site Indeed, in a media statement. Private sector employment fell by 53,000 positions last month, marking the first decline in the segment since February. Employment in the public sector, meanwhile, was up 50,000 positions. StatCan noted that, on a year-over-year basis, private sector jobs are still up while the public sector is down. Employment in the wholesale and retail trade industry has trended down over the past year and the sector led losses in October, shedding 29,000 roles. Transportation and warehousing and food and accommodation also posted losses last month, offset by some gains in construction and education. CIBC senior economist Andrew Grantham said in an interview that he had expected more of a lift in the October labour market from one-time factors like the Alberta referendum. While he had been anticipating the jobless rate would tick up in the fourth quarter in the face of tariff-related headwinds, Friday’s employment figures suggest there’s more underlying softness in the jobs market. “It does look as if we’re seeing some weakness in the labour market outside of those trade-sensitive areas. So that’s a concern for us right now,” Grantham said. That could dampen expectations for a rebound in job growth in 2027, he added. The unemployment rate for young workers aged 15 to 24 jumped to 13.7 per cent in October, up 0.7 percentage points from September, as employment edged down and more youth looked for work. Young workers have faced a generally tough labour market in recent years but there had been little change in the jobless rate for the age group over the summer. StatCan said the unemployment rate was higher for students compared with youth not attending school. The agency said the layoff rate – the proportion of people employed in September who were laid off by October – was “virtually unchanged” compared with a year earlier at 0.7 per cent. Average hourly wages rose 2.2 per cent annually in October, edging down from 2.3 per cent in September. Puri said Indeed’s Canadian job postings ticked up at the end of last month, which could be an indication of future hiring. If Canada can gain clarity on U.S. trade policy in the wake of the midterm elections this week, she said that could give employers the confidence to hire again. “If this optimism isn’t then translated into a strong jobs report in the months ahead, the surprising weakness in headline employment will start to look less temporary and more like the beginning of a renewed cooling in the labour market,” Puri warned. The October job figures come a little over a week after the Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike in more than three years, raising its policy rate by a quarter point to 2.5 per cent. Thomas Ryan, senior North America economist at Capital Economics, said in a note to clients that the uptick in the unemployment rate and muted wage growth should tell the Bank of Canada that there’s still slack in the job market right now. The October jobs data should therefore push back on calls for much more tightening of monetary policy, he argued. “Ultimately, this adds to our conviction that the bank will hike rates no more than twice more as a precaution against upside inflation risks, before calling it a day,” Ryan said. Financial market odds of another quarter-point hike at the Bank of Canada’s final rate decision of the year on Dec. 9 stood at 35 per cent as of Friday afternoon, according to LSEG Data & Analytics. Bank of Canada officials made clear after the October rate hike that their focus is on getting ahead of inflationary pressures spreading from the global energy shock, Grantham noted. Soft labour market data and recent declines in the benchmark price of oil take pressure of the central bank to deliver another rate hike next month, he said. “We have a lot of days for oil prices to do something volatile between now and December. But if those two forces stay in effect, we do forecast that they will hold interest rates at the December meeting,” Grantham said. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026. By Craig Lord

item.title: Telus targets $900M in annual cost savings as it sheds health, agriculture assets
item.description: Telus Corp. will look to find $900 million in annual cost savings by the end of 2028 as it divests non-core assets and seeks to “double down” on telecommunications investments.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: VANCOUVER — Telus Corp. will look to find $900 million in annual cost savings by the end of 2028 as it divests non-core assets and seeks to “double down” on telecommunications investments. Telus president and CEO Victor Dodig, who took the helm of the company in July, said in an interview on Friday that the cost reductions will come from “a combination of everything.” “A lot of it also has to do with the way we do business. So, for example, having our customers deal with issues through our app and modernizing our app and putting more self-serve out there,” said Dodig, who was previously chief executive of CIBC. “The banking sector has been very good at it, and I think the telecom sector can do more. It takes a lot of pressure points and pain points out for customers, so we can focus our time on the things that matter most to them, and that’s solving for their needs rather than solving for their problems.” By the end of 2028, the company expects to achieve a level of efficiencies equivalent to approximately $900 million in savings per year going forward. Around 80 per cent of the cash savings will come from the core telecom side of the company, with the balance from Telus’ global platform businesses. The company said the strategy focuses on improving customer service, customer growth and revenue per product. Achieving the lofty savings target by 2028 is one of the pillars of a transformation strategy unveiled Friday as the company reported its third-quarter results. The quarter saw Telus report a loss as it took an $800-million non-cash charge related to Telus Health. Dodig said the transformation is meant to strengthen Telus’ financial foundation, hone its operational discipline and control costs, and deploy resources to drive profitable and sustainable growth and returns. The strategy includes monetizing non-core assets, with a near-term priority on Telus Health and Telus Agriculture & Consumer Goods. Dodig said those businesses are “probably best in the hands of other capital providers over time so that we can take the resources that we free up and redeploy it into the Canadian telecom and digital infrastructure sector.” He said the company is already in “advanced discussions on one Telus Health asset” with a prospective buyer. “There’s just a broad thinking around, ‘How do we, as Telus, ensure that we maintain a position as the leader in telecom and digital infrastructure in Canada at a time where our country is facing an investment super cycle?’” he said. “How do we ... free up the resources that we have to redeploy into that industry that we think has really good growth and return prospects going forward?” While Telus sees potential growth from the telecom side, Dodig said that will require investment, noting over one million homes across Ontario and Quebec don’t yet have access to fibre internet, along with many in Western Canada. Telus will also look to build out its digital infrastructure, including through further investments in AI data centres. Earlier this year, the company announced plans for three B.C. facilities, adding to its factory in Rimouski, Que., that launched a year ago. In addition to those, it plans to leverage its fibre network to provide connectivity to data centres not owned by Telus. Telus said its loss attributable to common shares amounted to $667 million or 42 cents per share for the quarter ended Sept. 30 compared with a profit of $493 million or 32 cents per share a year ago. On an adjusted basis, Telus earned 16 cents per share in its latest quarter compared with an adjusted profit of 24 cents per share in the same quarter last year. Operating revenue and other income totalled $5.03 billion for the quarter, down from $5.11 billion a year ago. Dodig said Telus’ telecom business has shown signs of stabilization. Its total telecom subscriber connections for the quarter reached 18.3 million, up from 17.2 million in the third quarter of 2025. It added 84,000 net mobile phone subscribers in the quarter, an increase of 2,000 year-over-year. Its mobile phone churn rate — a measure of subscribers who cancelled their services — was 1.01 per cent in the quarter, an improvement from 1.11 per cent a year ago, which Telus said was largely due to its focus on customer retention and network quality, along with successful promotions. Mobile phone average revenue per user was $57.22 in the quarter, which was flat year-over-year. Telus reported it signed up 10,000 net internet customers, a decrease of 30,000 year-over-year, reflecting “a greater emphasis on premium and profitable” subscriptions. There were 289,000 connected device net additions, an increase of 120,000 year-over-year. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 6, 2026. By Sammy Hudes

item.title: U.S. employers added a surprising 165,000 jobs in October; unemployment rate dipped to 4.1%
item.description: U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 per cent.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: WASHINGTON — U.S. employers created a surprising 165,000 new jobs last month, and the unemployment rate dipped to 4.1 per cent. Hiring was far stronger than the 65,000 new jobs that economists had expected. The jobs report comes three days after voters delivered a stunning defeat to U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party in midterm elections. Frustrated with the state of the economy — and especially the high cost of living – Americans handed full control of Congress to the Democrats. But the latest jobs report looked solid. Labor Department revisions added a combined 84,000 new jobs to the August and September totals. The unemployment rate fell even though 421,000 people entered the labour force. Average hourly wages rose 0.4 per cent in October from September, the biggest month-over-month gain since January. “This was a blowout jobs report,’’ said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones. “Payroll growth exceeded expectations, revisions were positive, the unemployment rate fell, participation improved, and wage growth strengthened.’’ The strong job gains will likely make Federal Reserve policymakers more confident in the health of the labour market, giving them leeway to focus on persistently high inflation and raise their benchmark interest rate at their next meeting in December. The central bank typically seeks to bring down inflation by lifting its key interest rate to cool borrowing and spending. The Fed raised the rate in September but left it alone at its meeting last month. Wall Street investors now see the chance of a December rate hike at 77 per cent, up about 10 percentage points from Thursday, according to CME’s FedWatch. “For sure, we’re looking at another rate increase in December and possibly another one in early 2027,’’ said Boston College economist Brian Bethune. Solid hiring also underscores a concern among many Fed officials that their key rate isn’t high enough to slow inflation. Hourly wages were up a meager 3.1 per cent from October 2025. That means many workers have seen their purchasing power decline over the past year, despite continued hiring. Professional and business services – a broad category of administrative and managerial workers – added 70,000 jobs. Healthcare companies hired nearly 42,000. Factories added 19,000 jobs. But hotels, restaurants and bars cut 10,600. The job market has been solid but unspectacular. So far this year, employers — companies, government agencies and nonprofits — have added an average of 86,000 jobs a month. That is modest by historic standards but an improvement over 2025, when monthly job creation averaged 9,700. That was the weakest performance outside of a recession since 2002. Last year, high interest rates and U.S. President Donald Trump’s unpredictable trade policies discouraged hiring. Despite recovering this year, hiring remains well below the average of 166,000 jobs created monthly in 2023 and 2024, let alone the 491,000 a month recorded during the 2021-2022 hiring boom that followed COVID-19 lockdowns. Economists see a “low-hire, low-fire’’ environment in which employers are reluctant to let go of existing workers but aren’t in any hurry to hire new ones. Young people entering the workforce, or those who’ve lost their jobs, can struggle to find work. The United States doesn’t need as many new jobs as it once did to keep the unemployment rate from rising. That’s because baby boomer retirements and Trump’s immigration crackdown mean fewer people are competing for work. In late 2023, the so-called break-even point was around 166,000 new jobs a month. It’s now just over 5,000, according to an estimate by Yale University’s Budget Lab, which drew on an earlier Federal Reserve report. The American economy and job market have proven resilient in the face of a series of shocks — Trump’s double-digit tariffs on imports and the war with Iran, which has driven U.S. gasoline prices above US$4 a gallon and pinched family budgets. Gross domestic product — the nation’s output of goods and services — advanced at a sprightly 3.4 per cent annual pace from July through September, lifted by strong consumer spending and booming investment in artificial intelligence. But AI can also mean that businesses need fewer workers. At SharkNinja in Needham, Massachusetts, sales jumped 21 per cent in the latest quarter as budget-minded shoppers brought the company’s appliances – such as coffee- and smoothie-makers-- to save money on dining out. But CEO Mark Barrocas says he’s slowed hiring – to 5 per cent next year from 8 per cent to 10 per cent the previous two years. The reason: AI. SharkNinja, which has a total global work force of 4,200, has implemented AI tools in such areas as product innovation, media planning and finance. “It’s allowing people to work on much more higher impact initiatives as opposed to more tedious tasks,” he said. But AI has also created new jobs for people with expertise in using AI to increase efficiency. ____ Paul Wiseman, The Associated Press AP Retail Writer Anne D’Innocenzio in New York and AP Economics Writer Christopher Rugaber contributed to this story.
